/uk-news/2026/nov/16/police-retreating-f.headline: Ethnic minority groups in Wales four times more likely to be target of police facial scans
/uk-news/2026/nov/16/police-retreating-f.excerpt: Ethnic minority people are four times more likely than their white counterparts to be chosen for some police facial scans, according to official data, sparking warnings of racial bias. Internal figures released by South Wales police revealed that 24% of people selected by police for facial recognition checks were from ethnic minorities, despite this group making up only 7% of the area’s total population. The force polices Wales’s largest cities – Cardiff and Swansea – and has pioneered several versions of AI-enabled facial recognition technology. The latest figures relate to police officers capturing a person’s face with a smartphone and running the image through an algorithm called “Neoface” to match it against custody mugshots and other face databases. Most scans are made because people are suspected of crimes. Civil liberties campaigners called the ethnicity figures “alarming”. The force said they raised “concerns about disproportionality” and that it was reviewing its approach. The data relates to a full year of use in 2025 and was obtained under the Freedom of Information Act and shared with the Guardian. Even when compared with arrest data for the police area, in which 11% of people arrested are from ethnic minorities, the face-scan figures appear disproportionate.
/uk-news/2026/nov/16/police-retreating-f.trail: Exclusive: South Wales police figures show BAME people accounted for 24% of selected scans in 2025, despite being 7% of population

/uk-news/2026/nov/16/police-retreating-f.headline: Police to target 500 chronic shoplifters in retail crime crackdown in England
/uk-news/2026/nov/16/police-retreating-f.excerpt: Five hundred of the most prolific shoplifters across England will be targeted in a police crackdown on retail crime, with tougher sentences, high street bans and GPS tagging. The home secretary, Shabana Mahmood, said up to 17 police forces would target the repeat offenders in their area, collecting evidence of offences to secure stronger sentences and ensure they face “real consequences”, backed by an extra £2.5m in funding. Tactics will include the expanded use of criminal behaviour orders – where repeat offenders are banned from high streets and town centres – GPS tagging and intensive supervision courts, where perpetrators must attend regular judicial hearings. Those who do not comply or breach conditions will face imprisonment in the most serious cases, and foreign offenders could face deportation. Mahmood said the government wanted to target people “who are causing so much harm to our communities”. She said: “A small number of offenders commit a disproportionate amount of shop theft. They wreak havoc on our high streets, leave businesses out of pocket and make retail workers scared to go to work.” The government said it wanted to replicate the success of Operation Kelleher, a targeted crackdown on 10 shoplifters in Bromley in 2025 that reduced recorded retail crime in the area by 70%, according to Metropolitan police data. The number of shoplifting offences recorded by police in England and Wales rose to the highest on record in 2024, surpassing half a million offences.
/uk-news/2026/nov/16/police-retreating-f.trail: Tactics to include GPS tagging for repeat offenders, high street bans and tougher sentences

/uk-news/2026/nov/16/police-retreating-f.headline: Russell Brand suspected to have attacked at least 10 other women
/uk-news/2026/nov/16/police-retreating-f.excerpt: Police are bracing themselves for more victims of Russell Brand to come forward, with at least 10 more women suspected of having been attacked by the disgraced star. Brand, 51, will be sentenced on Monday to what is expected to be a lengthy jail sentence for rape and sexual assaults after he abused his fame to become a “predator” targeting women, and got away with it for years. The fallout from Brand’s case saw the government pledge to examine calls to crack down on “rape myths” in trials. The Guardian also understands that next week the Metropolitan police team that built the case against Brand will start sifting through reports and intelligence about other potential victims. The Met commissioner, Sir Mark Rowley, said there could be “many more” victims, but declined to say how many, with some intelligence about further victims being third-hand and some further suspected victims reluctant to face the criminal justice system. Sources say it is feared the number of further victims is at least in “double digits”, with 10 currently seen as a minimum. The Met police said on Thursday that Brand was under investigation for two further rape allegations. Detectives have sent files to specialist rape prosecutors and are in discussions with them over the material. Rowley said: “We’ve got two other victims who’ve come forward who want to tell their story, and so two rape cases we’re investigating.
/uk-news/2026/nov/16/police-retreating-f.trail: Met police chief says ‘many more’ victims could come forward, as actor and comedian awaits sentencing

/uk-news/2026/nov/16/police-retreating-f.headline: Police chief condemns ‘terrifying’ Bonfire Night violence across Scotland
/uk-news/2026/nov/16/police-retreating-f.excerpt: A police chief has condemned the “unacceptable and terrifying” Bonfire Night disorder that resulted in seven arrests, a police van being torched and an officer and a paramedic being injured. Ch Supt David Robertson of Police Scotland said there had been significant reduction in problems overall, compared with 2025, after the force deployed its largest number of officers since Donald Trump’s visit last year. However, a police officer and ambulance worker sustained minor injuries after being attacked with fireworks while they were responding to a report of an injured man in Greenside Street, Glasgow. A police van was then gutted after being set on fire in the same street in the Provanmill area of the city, where a 16-year-old boy was also arrested. In south-west Edinburgh, the Scottish fire and rescue service (SFRS) had to withdraw after trying to put out bin fires set by young local people. In England, police arrested six people in North Shields near Newcastle upon Tyne after a number of officers were injured, with police and fire service vehicles damaged after fireworks and bricks were thrown at them. A large group of people had gathered outside a supermarket after wrongly being told it was going to be a house of multiple occupancy (HMO). As part of Operation Amberlight, Police Scotland had tried to prevent a recurrence of the violence that erupted in Edinburgh and Glasgow last year.
/uk-news/2026/nov/16/police-retreating-f.trail: Emergency services attacked and police van set alight in Glasgow, while disorder also erupts in north-east England

/uk-news/2026/nov/16/police-retreating-f.headline: Flashbulbs, lies and victim blaming: how Russell Brand’s trial unfolded
/uk-news/2026/nov/16/police-retreating-f.excerpt: Russell Brand’s trial at Southwark crown court, which ended with him being found guilty of raping one woman and sexually assaulting three others, was one of the most obsessively watched criminal cases in recent history. As well as Brand’s own conduct, the case became an examination of his victims’ evidence, the legal strategy his team used to defend him, and the culture within which he committed his crimes. The victims: ‘I remember him on me. I know I said no’ Brand’s victims told how he “snapped” from charming to nasty as he raped and sexually assaulted them before gaslighting them into believing nothing was wrong. The comedian’s youngest victim, who was 21 when he targeted her at the height of his fame in 2009, was left traumatised by their encounter. Brand had stored her name in his phone alongside a series of letters and symbols. The court heard the letter “T” stood for “tart”, while “AP” denoted anal play, and two asterisks meant: “Never, ever forget this individual, this is a memorable encounter.” It was, indeed, an encounter the woman would never forget, she spent years torturing and blaming herself for what happened. The woman was starstruck when she met Brand after one of his standup performances at the Hammersmith Apollo in early 2009. Brand, who was more than a decade her senior, picked the woman from the crowd and invited her to his dressing room. There, she performed oral sex on him and engaged in a threesome with another young fan.
/uk-news/2026/nov/16/police-retreating-f.trail: Level of interest in comedian’s case resulted in examination of affairs inside and outside the courtroom

/society/2026/nov/16/alan-milburn-urges-.headline: Burnham pledges early intervention and ‘benefits backstop’ to tackle youth jobs crisis
/society/2026/nov/16/alan-milburn-urges-.excerpt: Andy Burnham has pledged to intervene as early as childhood to tackle youth unemployment before a watershed review, promising “a root-and-branch rethink of how we support childhood in the modern world”. Burnham said the government would intervene at all the stages of life in which young people fell behind, and “long before they find themselves out of work and reliant on the state”, including providing more opportunities for vocational training in schools. Writing in the Guardian, the prime minister said ministers’ response to Alan Milburn’s long-awaited review into the crisis of youth unemployment in the UK would not be “a traditional … reform” but “societal and generational”. He promised to reduce the number of Neets – 18- to 24-year-olds not in employment, education or training – which topped a million this year for the first time in more than a decade. Hoping to head off opposition from leftwing MPs in his own party, who rebelled to block Starmer’s welfare changes last summer, Burnham said the government would “invest in our young people and give them a proper chance to get on”, but said the support “will have to come with responsibilities”. “If we give young people genuine opportunities to learn, train and work, we should expect them to take them where they can. Benefits must become the backstop, not the starting point,” said Burnham.
/society/2026/nov/16/alan-milburn-urges-.trail: Prime minister promises ‘root-and branch rethink’ of support for young people as Milburn report advises sweeping changes to some benefits

/society/2026/nov/16/alan-milburn-urges-.headline: ‘The social contract is broken’: young people on feeling shut out of careers
/society/2026/nov/16/alan-milburn-urges-.excerpt: ‘You can do everything right and still lose’ – Aamir, 25 “I’ve been demoralised by the process, just constantly applying, then interviewing. I’ve just been applying to any jobs that I could find. I’d really like to be employed by now. Some companies don’t even give rejection emails … they’re not obligated to reply to the prospective interviewee, but they should be compelled to.” By Aamir’s estimate, he has applied for more than 1,000 jobs since graduating last year. The 25-year-old has a BA in media and communications and an MA in media studies from two Russell group London universities. He landed a temporary digital publishing role at a media company, but the contract ended after a few months. Two years later, he is living with his parents in east London, claiming universal credit and looking for work. “I would like to not be on benefits,” he says. “I would like to have a proper entry-level job in what I studied, but I haven’t been able to get anything. I’m trying.” Aamir also attends interview coaching through the government’s Restart programme and is completing free Google qualifications to strengthen his CV. “The universal credit people told me I’d done everything right,” he says. “You can do everything right and still lose. “I feel like the social contract is broken in Britain.
/society/2026/nov/16/alan-milburn-urges-.trail: In the first instalment of a new series, four young people reveal the impact of an endless cycle of applications and rejections

/society/2026/nov/16/alan-milburn-urges-.headline: Some young disabled people to lose Pip in Milburn plan – but can apply to local fund
/society/2026/nov/16/alan-milburn-urges-.excerpt: Some young people with disabilities will lose their personal independence payments but will be able to apply to a local fund for short-term expenses and equipment, Alan Milburn’s review will recommend. While those with the most severe needs’ entitlement will be protected, others will be asked to apply for money for specific purposes rather than an ongoing payment. Under-25s will be no longer eligible to claim Pip and the health element of universal credit and instead will get a new youth allowance paid at the standard rate of universal credit. Milburn, a former health secretary, has said the current system of benefits must be entirely replaced for young people. “We need to tear up the old approach and start again for under-25s. A tweak to the benefits system just won’t do,” he said in a statement to the Guardian announcing the plans. “We need a new system built around a young person with schools, the NHS and employers all working together to make sure that everyone has the chance to earn or learn.” The long-awaited report on youth unemployment will promise almost half a million job and education opportunities within a decade, but will also advise sweeping changes to the benefits system for under-25s. There will be a local fund for young people with disabilities to apply to for money to pay for equipment or for help with short-term expenses such as travel to attend a training course or job interview, the Guardian understands.
/society/2026/nov/16/alan-milburn-urges-.trail: Exclusive: Former health secretary wants to ‘tear up the old approach’, and end ongoing payments to certain under-25s

/society/2026/nov/16/alan-milburn-urges-.headline: Fixing UK’s youth jobs crisis demands much more investment, TUC boss warns
/society/2026/nov/16/alan-milburn-urges-.excerpt: Fixing Britain’s youth jobs crisis will require ministers to drastically increase investment in employment support while avoiding arbitrary cuts to benefits, the head of the trade union movement has said. Before an important official report expected next week, the general secretary of the Trades Union Congress, Paul Nowak, said the government had a “once in a generation chance” to secure young people’s futures. In an interview with the Guardian before the highly anticipated Milburn review into young people and work, he said the costs of increasing job support, education and training would be outweighed by economic gains that would help to ease the pressure on the welfare state. “There is no solution that is cost-free,” he said. “The government is going to have to be prepared to invest in securing the future of those young people, but also to invest to secure what is the future of our economy. “This is where the government is going to have to be clear. Of course as a country it’s right to invest in our physical infrastructure, but also we have to invest in social infrastructure too.” Ministers are braced for the report by Alan Milburn, the former Labour health secretary, to recommend welfare cuts to fund job support for almost a million young people who are not in education, employment or training (Neet).
/society/2026/nov/16/alan-milburn-urges-.trail: Paul Nowak also calls on government to avoid arbitrary benefit cuts before much-anticipated Milburn report is published this week

/society/2026/nov/16/alan-milburn-urges-.headline: Starbucks plans to hire 7,500 staff in major UK expansion plan
/society/2026/nov/16/alan-milburn-urges-.excerpt: Starbucks has set out plans to hire 7,500 new baristas over the next five years, in a boost to youth employment as the chain pins hopes for future growth on the north of the country. The US coffee shop chain, which employs more than 18,000 people in the UK, said the hiring spree would focus on the Midlands, north of England, Wales and Scotland, as it targets growth north of the M25. The roles are expected to staff 500 new coffee shops which Starbucks hopes to open across the country by 2031. The company set out the growth plan earlier this year after shutting dozens of underperforming outlets in Britain last year as part of a $1bn (£750m) global restructuring. Darren King, who runs Starbucks UK, said: “We’re deeply focused on how we can help more young people into these positions, starting by making entry-level roles as accessible as possible.” Starbucks is a large youth employer and set out its plan before an official report into the number of young people not in education, employment or training, known as Neets, which hit a record high above 1 million at the start of the year. The rise in worklessness was dealt a blow in the run-up to the budget last month, as UK employers cut back on hiring amid worries about rising costs and the outlook for the British economy, according to a monthly survey.
/society/2026/nov/16/alan-milburn-urges-.trail: Coffee shop chain targets growth north of London with extra 500 outlets in big boost for youth employment

/news/2026/nov/16/ministry-of-justice-in.headline: Barristers could be barred from practice over use of rape myths, warns justice secretary
/news/2026/nov/16/ministry-of-justice-in.excerpt: Barristers could be barred from practice if they perpetuate rape myths to defend clients, the justice secretary has said after Russell Brand’s trial. Alex Norris has written to the body that regulates barristers amid concern over the tactics deployed by the comedian’s counsel. In his letter to the Bar Standards Board (BSB), Norris said it was “unacceptable” for the profession to “perpetuate myths” about rape victims in court, and warned that those who broke the rules could face disciplinary action. A series of rape myths were allegedly deployed in the defence of Brand, 51, during his trial at Southwark crown court, including the argument that his accusers should not be believed because they had not screamed, kicked or fled. Brand was convicted of attacks against four of the six women who gave evidence against him, and is serving a 10-and-a-half-year prison term for one count of rape and three sexual assaults. In his closing speech to the jury, Brand’s defence barrister, Ian Winter KC, argued that the comedian could not be a rapist because his accusers had not “resisted or screamed or even tried to leave”. Winter asked the jury whether they could be sure that of the “many, many women” Brand had slept with over a decade, he had “raped just three of them”. Winter has reported himself to the BSB after criticisms over an exchange with a Sunday Times journalist outside court as well as his conduct within it.
/news/2026/nov/16/ministry-of-justice-in.trail: Move follows Russell Brand trial, in which his barrister argued comedian could not be a rapist because his accusers had not ‘resisted’

/news/2026/nov/16/ministry-of-justice-in.headline: Is it finally OK to be frank about 2000s pop culture? ‘It was profoundly, cheerfully horrible to women’
/news/2026/nov/16/ministry-of-justice-in.excerpt: In a 2008 episode of BBC Two’s comedy panel show Never Mind the Buzzcocks, the choreographer Arlene Phillips – the only woman on the programme – was told by the host Simon Amstell: “You look like you run a good whore house.” In reply, Phillips told a story with what appeared to be faux sincerity: while working with big stars, she explained, she would sometimes be asked to find dancers with “very special abilities” who might want to party after filming. Another panellist, the TV presenter Dermot O’Leary, mimed picking up a phone and said: “When you’re dancing tonight, do you mind having sex afterwards?” Everyone laughed. Russell Brand’s imprisonment for rape and sexual assault this week, and allegations of sexual misconduct against the comedian and children’s author David Walliams have prompted scrutiny not only of the men involved, but of those who appeared to enable them. The chatshow host Jonathan Ross has apologised for a 2004 joke, in which he described the 15-year-old British comedy awards as being “like most 15-year-olds: drunk, unpredictable and probably going home with David Walliams”. The latter has denied the allegations made against him in reporting by the Guardian and ITV News, but is now the focus of an investigation by the Met police on separate sexual misconduct claims. On the face of it, Phillips’s story had nothing to do with Brand or Walliams. But as clips like this have resurfaced they have been viewed in a different light.
/news/2026/nov/16/ministry-of-justice-in.trail: The imprisonment of Russell Brand and allegations against David Walliams have prompted scrutiny of a culture that encouraged male transgression

/news/2026/nov/16/ministry-of-justice-in.headline: Two courtrooms, one celebrity: how did the Russell Brand case compare with the rape trial next door?
/news/2026/nov/16/ministry-of-justice-in.excerpt: What is going on inside Russell Brand’s head as he arrives at court for the start of his rape trial? He sees the dozens of cameras and journalists lined outside Southwark crown court, many of whom have been waiting since before 7am, and he tells himself that the media are all against him. “It seems to me that they believe that I am guilty, and that this should be the rubber-stamping of the process of my destruction.” He walks with his wife, Laura, and his bodyguard past the photographers, “clickering, clackering, snickering paparazzi, like locusts, peculiar concoctions, not fully humans”, and up into the court, where he is suddenly overwhelmed by “the presence of something very beautiful, grace”. “In a situation like I’m in, it’s impossible not to turn to God. Truth and justice are the only things that can save me,” he thinks. In one of the early hearings, he also receives some words of support from a court security guard, “just some normal geezer, patting me down for weapons or sharps”, who whispers: “All right, Russell. The whole country’s behind you, mate. The whole country’s behind you.” Brand takes solace from these words. “I felt very, very encouraged.” I’m not a mind reader, so how do I know all this? Usually we know nothing about the thoughts of defendants in trials because they stay silent for the duration, but Brand finds it hard to stay quiet.
/news/2026/nov/16/ministry-of-justice-in.trail: One was a high-profile defendant watched by more than 100 journalists. Another was an unknown man who preyed on a girl almost half his age. Their stories played out minutes apart, one entirely out of the spotlight

/news/2026/nov/16/ministry-of-justice-in.headline: Russell Brand accused of misconduct by six more women, according to report
/news/2026/nov/16/ministry-of-justice-in.excerpt: Russell Brand has been accused of sexual misconduct and predatory behaviour by a further six women, according to a report. The comedian, 51, is accused of having sex with a woman without her consent and then apologising afterwards, an investigation by the Times and the Sunday Times said. The newspapers also alleged the comedian continued having sex with another woman after she asked him to stop because he was hurting her. Brand, 51, was sentenced to more than 10 years in prison on Monday after being convicted of raping a 21-year-old fan and sexually assaulting three women in separate incidents between 2004 and 2009. He was cleared of two further charges of rape and one of attempted indecent assault at Southwark crown court in London. The Times reported that a woman said she had an on-off relationship with the actor in the late 2000s after a professional meeting at his London home. On one occasion, she said they were in bed together when he moved to initiate sex. Having noticed he was not wearing a condom, she said she asked him to stop. She told the Times: “And then he was very close, on top of me, and sort of pushing – but I knew he didn’t have a condom on and I said: ‘No, stop,’ and I started to sort of try and move. And … that wasn’t happening.” The woman added she decided at that moment that “I’m not going to fight” because “who knows what he could do”. After the alleged incident, she said Brand apologised to her in person and by text message.
/news/2026/nov/16/ministry-of-justice-in.trail: Allegations of sexual misconduct and predatory behaviour made against ex-comedian who was jailed on Monday

/film/2026/nov/16/new-james-bond-announc.headline: Robert Pattinson’s journey from Harry Potter and Twilight to James Bond: ‘The honour of a lifetime’
/film/2026/nov/16/new-james-bond-announc.excerpt: There are big years in an actor’s career, and then there is Robert Pattinson’s 2026. This year the 40-year-old Briton has been the face of everything from Kristoffer Borgli’s relationship satire The Drama to Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey and Lance Oppenheim’s Primetime. Now, in the culmination of a remarkable run, he has landed the most coveted role in British cinema: James Bond. After weeks of intense speculation, on Monday the official Bond accounts confirmed Pattinson as the seventh actor to play 007. “James Bond is one of the most legendary characters in cinema, and to be entrusted with 007 is the honour of a lifetime,” Pattinson said. Pattinson was easily the most famous of the contenders, and an unusual one: an arthouse actor with a franchise heart-throb’s profile. “Is Robert Pattinson the last true movie star?” the New York Times asked in 2024. Pattinson landed his first big film role more than two decades ago, playing Cedric Diggory in 2005’s Harry Potter and the Goblet of Fire. He became a household name at 21, when he was cast opposite Kristen Stewart in the first of five Twilight films. The pair played star-crossed lovers Edward Cullen, a vampire, and Bella Swan, a mortal – turning Pattinson into a global teen pin-up. The on-screen romance also became a real-life one: the pair dated for four years, as the films became a global phenomenon, eventually taking more than $3.3bn at the worldwide box office.
/film/2026/nov/16/new-james-bond-announc.trail: The 40-year-old British actor has had a remarkable career and is back again with the coveted 007

/uk-news/2026/nov/16/failed-uk-asylum-se.headline: Planned asylum seeker detention centre next to Oxfordshire sewage works criticised
/uk-news/2026/nov/16/failed-uk-asylum-se.excerpt: A Home Office plan to build asylum seeker detention facilities next to a sewage pump is facing objections after water company officials warned that detainees should expect to experience insect swarms and strong smells. Proposed secure accommodation blocks at Campsfield House immigration removal centre in Oxfordshire will be 20 metres from a sewage pumping station, according to a written submission from Thames Water. A senior development manager at the company wrote that it could give rise to “amenity effects, including odour, noise, vibration, lighting associated with maintenance activities, insects and flies” for any inhabitants. In a previous submission, the company wrote that any development may lead to sewage flooding. The warnings, which come as the government hopes to expand the immigration detention estate by 40%, have been seized upon by campaigners against the expansion. Ally Swadling, the lead legal education officer at the charity Right to Remain, said: “Thames Water’s concerns about sewage infrastructure at Campsfield show how little regard is being given to even the most basic standards of sanitation and human dignity. “They reinforce what we already know – this government is putting its political priorities above people’s lives and wellbeing.” The centre near Kidlington re-opened in December 2025 after it was shut in 2018 following years of problems, including suicides, riots, escapes and complaints about conditions.
/uk-news/2026/nov/16/failed-uk-asylum-se.trail: Thames Water says detainees at proposed Oxfordshire accommodation should expect to experience insect swarms and strong smells

/uk-news/2026/nov/16/failed-uk-asylum-se.headline: Torture survivors may have been sent to Sussex asylum camp unlawfully, documentary reveals
/uk-news/2026/nov/16/failed-uk-asylum-se.excerpt: Asylum seekers accommodated at a controversial military base in East Sussex have been subjected to inadequate welfare checks, and torture survivors may have been placed there unlawfully, an undercover documentary for ITV has revealed. Mass accommodation sites are central to the government’s plan to end the use of hotels to house asylum seekers. For the documentary, Inside The Asylum Camp, ITV’s undercover reporter got a job as a welfare officer at Crowborough and covertly filmed inside the former military training camp. The documentary claims that poor screening and welfare checks are having serious consequences for some of the asylum seekers. This May, the high court ruled that a Home Office policy change forcing torture survivors to share rooms was unlawful. The accommodation at Crowborough is in large dormitories. The Home Office’s decision to accommodate asylum seekers on two former military sites – Crowborough, and Wethersfield in Essex – has triggered opposition from local residents. Plans to use three other sites – Bicester, Barnham and Linton-on-Ouse – have caused a similar outcry, mostly around fears about asylum seekers causing a rise in violent crime. However, very low levels of even minor crimes have been recorded by police at Wethersfield and Crowborough among asylum seekers at the two camps. The Crowborough site is run by Clearsprings Ready Homes.
/uk-news/2026/nov/16/failed-uk-asylum-se.trail: Undercover ITV report also shows inadequate welfare checks at ex-military base run by firm of asylum camp billionaire Graham King

/uk-news/2026/nov/16/failed-uk-asylum-se.headline: UK tells blind Nigerian pensioner to go to India for medical treatment
/uk-news/2026/nov/16/failed-uk-asylum-se.excerpt: A blind Nigerian pensioner who has lived in the UK for 26 years has been told by the Home Office she can safely go to India, a country she has never visited, for medical treatment. Comfort*, 67, arrived in the UK in 2000, and shortly after suddenly went blind due to acute glaucoma. After living here for 20 years, she was granted leave to remain under long residence rules. Those allowed to stay on this route have to renew their visa every 30 months for 10 years and after that can apply for indefinite leave to remain. Under the new settlement rules announced by Shabana Mahmood this week, it is likely Comfort will now have to keep renewing her visa for the next 20 years before she will finally, when she reaches her 80s, be eligible for indefinite leave to remain. Due to her age and disability, lawyers at Refugee and Migrant Justice applied to the Home Office for her to be granted indefinite leave to remain now rather than having to wait two more decades before becoming eligible. There is a provision to fast-track indefinite leave to remain applications in exceptional circumstances. However, the Home Office rejected this application, telling her in the first part of the letter that she could return to Nigeria because there are services there for blind people.
/uk-news/2026/nov/16/failed-uk-asylum-se.trail: Woman who has lived in UK for 26 years refused indefinite leave to remain under Home Office’s new settlement rules

/uk-news/2026/nov/16/failed-uk-asylum-se.headline: Angela Rayner grants planning approval for asylum centre in Piddington despite local opposition
/uk-news/2026/nov/16/failed-uk-asylum-se.excerpt: The communities secretary, Angela Rayner, has approved full planning permission for an asylum centre at a Ministry of Defence site near the village of Piddington in Oxfordshire. The decision approves plans to go ahead with the refurbishment and redevelopment of the former barracks. The Home Office insists that final approval is still to be determined. In September, people in Piddington voted to leave the UK in a symbolic referendum against plans to house 1,256 detained asylum seekers nearby. A total of 285 people were in favour of independence from the UK while 26 voted against. The poll was organised by campaigners for residents to demonstrate opposition to the plans for accommodation at the converted MoD site near the town of Bicester. A Home Office spokesperson said on Thursday: “Planning permission allows us to continue to progress the use of MoD Bicester. However, a final decision to proceed is yet to be taken. “The government is working on a fairer distribution of asylum accommodation across the country, with over £1bn saved in costs since the election. “This includes closing all asylum hotels and moving to alternative accommodation, including former military sites. These are designed to be self-contained, with 24/7 security and CCTV, to minimise the impact on the local community.” There is now a six-week window when the decision can face a legal challenge.

/uk-news/2026/nov/16/failed-uk-asylum-se.headline: Mahmood’s ICE-style immigration raid agency accused of ‘fishing expeditions’
/uk-news/2026/nov/16/failed-uk-asylum-se.excerpt: Shabana Mahmood’s ICE-style raid agency has been accused of engaging in “fishing expeditions” after figures disclosed that almost two-thirds of enforcement visits result in no arrests and nearly three-quarters are conducted without a warrant. The home secretary has hailed the expanded use of immigration enforcement teams, and claimed they will help to secure the UK’s borders by removing a key incentive for irregular migration. Under her leadership, raids have targeted establishments associated with informal “black market” work such as nail bars, car washes, barbers, takeaways, construction sites and warehouses, as well as people’s homes. They have been accompanied by videos posted on TikTok showing arrests of people working without authorisation being tackled to the ground by enforcement officers and locked in the back of vans. Freedom of information requests, however, show that: There were 23,538 immigration enforcement engagements such as workplace raids, home raids and spot checks in 2025 – or 60 a day. Of these, 15,578, or 66.1%, resulted in no arrests. Only 25.81% of visits where a premises was accessed used a warrant. Critics say this suggests the Home Office is launching “fishing expeditions” based on weak intelligence. Nearly nine out of 10 (89%) of leads alleging “immigration crime” in 2025 came from the public or from Crimestoppers, a charity that collects anonymous tip-offs. Around 2% came from the police.

/tv-and-radio/2026/nov/16/woman-accusing.headline: Russell Brand accused of misconduct by six more women, according to report
/tv-and-radio/2026/nov/16/woman-accusing.excerpt: Russell Brand has been accused of sexual misconduct and predatory behaviour by a further six women, according to a report. The comedian, 51, is accused of having sex with a woman without her consent and then apologising afterwards, an investigation by the Times and the Sunday Times said. The newspapers also alleged the comedian continued having sex with another woman after she asked him to stop because he was hurting her. Brand, 51, was sentenced to more than 10 years in prison on Monday after being convicted of raping a 21-year-old fan and sexually assaulting three women in separate incidents between 2004 and 2009. He was cleared of two further charges of rape and one of attempted indecent assault at Southwark crown court in London. The Times reported that a woman said she had an on-off relationship with the actor in the late 2000s after a professional meeting at his London home. On one occasion, she said they were in bed together when he moved to initiate sex. Having noticed he was not wearing a condom, she said she asked him to stop. She told the Times: “And then he was very close, on top of me, and sort of pushing – but I knew he didn’t have a condom on and I said: ‘No, stop,’ and I started to sort of try and move. And … that wasn’t happening.” The woman added she decided at that moment that “I’m not going to fight” because “who knows what he could do”. After the alleged incident, she said Brand apologised to her in person and by text message.
